summary: Sydney Harbour's east-side light since 1832 on Low Point (Flat Point), New Waterford; the octagonal concrete tower dates from 1938 and is a federal heritage building.

corrections.why: The light has been shown from the point since 1832; 1938 is the date of the present tower, not of first light.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1832 (first light, station established) and 1938 (present tower). Both are sourced: the light was first shown in 1832; the concrete tower was built in 1938 and reuses the lantern and lens of the old wooden tower.

The Coast Guard list gives Fl W 5s (a single flash). The 1908 lens gave a double flash, per the Chance Heritage Trust, so the characteristic changed after 1908 (or the 1908 description and the present list differ in how they are read). Both are recorded in the events.

notes_for_editor: (1) The 1832-1833 history (petition, tender, keepers, the 1833 gale and cold) rests on two secondary accounts, the Chance Heritage Trust and LighthouseFriends, which give almost the same wording. Neither was checked against the Journal of the House of Assembly. The story says so only by its sourcing. (2) Keeper name: the Trust's narrative says Michael McKeagney; its keeper list and LighthouseFriends print George McKeagney. The story uses Michael and gives the Trust's keeper list as George. (3) Jobe's start: the Trust's narrative says 1979; its own keeper list and LighthouseFriends say 1978. The roster uses 1978; the story states both. (4) Society founding: the Trust gives 2014 in its excerpt and 2012 in its body (LighthouseFriends says 2012). The story leaves the year out. (5) Lens and lantern: the register says the 1938 tower reuses an iron lantern recovered from the 1832 tower and keeps the 'original' lens system; the Trust says the 1908 lantern room and lens came from the old wooden tower, and that a rotating airport beacon replaced the Fresnel lens in 1984. Unresolved; both views are in the story. (6) Tower height disagrees: the Coast Guard lists 20.8 m (tower, 'White octagonal tower with red top'); the Trust's data sheet gives 22 m (72 ft). The story states both. (7) The 1909 report (Flat Point, printed p. 56) is the primary confirmation of the 1908-09 lantern change. (8) Keepers from 1952 onward (O'Neill, MacDonald, Tanner, Jobe) ended after about 1960: names and years only, as the published lists print them; no family or personal details. (9) Jobe's wife and the private lease of the surviving dwelling are in the Trust's page; left out. (10) The 1901 inspector remark is in a numbered list in the report (printed p. 32, the inspection section). (11) Wikidata's 1938 first_lit entry is corrected in the corrections list; the light has been shown since 1832. (12) The 'Nordcaper' trawler (a 1911 distress off Low Point) was seen in the corpus but its date and page could not be confirmed in the OCR, so it is not used. (13) Sources reviewed: the Canadian Register's listing gives the recognition date of 19 October 2006 and calls the tower a Recognized Federal Heritage Building, not a national historic site. (14) The Myrtle F. Hopkins entry (16 November 1909, printed p. 51) gives the place as 'Lowpoint' in a Cape Breton list of the same tug's work; the story says 'probably this point', because the report does not say so. (15) The Trust's and the report's quotations are indirect in two places: the McKeagney remark ('fit for a dog') and the McNab 1857 remark are the Trust's own words, not quotations from the keepers, so the story does not put them in quotation marks. (16) PAGES: the 1901 inspection entry is printed p. 32 (the header precedes the entry); the 1903 Cranberry Head note is printed p. 61 (scan p. 74); the 1909 Flat Point lantern entry is printed p. 56 (scan p. 63); the 1909 tug line for Ronald L. Smith is printed p. 34 (scan p. 41) in the Deputy Minister's report; the 1910 Myrtle entry is printed p. 51 (scan p. 51).
